prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a continuous front-to-back gradient across a cluttered wooden table directly in front of and below the camera wearer (0.3 to 1.2 m away), behind which a person sits at the far edge (about 1.2 to 1.5 m away) in front of a shelving unit and window wall (2.5 to 3.5 m away) and a distant living area with a second seated person on the far left (about 4 to 5 m away). Near-edge tabletop items—including jars, a butter dish, a white paper-towel roll on the left, and a dark water bottle in the center—appear bright white within the camera wearer's arm's reach (0.3 to 0.8 m) and partially occlude the table surface and the seated person's lower body, while the closed laptop on the right (0.8 to 1.0 m) and cards/laptop in front of the seated person are within that person's reach. Across frames 1 to 5, as the camera wearer turns their head slightly rightward and tilts upward in frames 4 and 5, the foreground table and seated person shift leftward in the frame and grow slightly darker (retreating from roughly 1.2 m to 1.5 m), while a bright vertical doorframe and appliance enter on the far right edge at about 0.5 to 1.0 m and the far-left room rotates out of view. Compared to RGB alone, the depth map clearly separates the vertical silhouettes of the paper-towel roll and water bottle from the cluttered tabletop behind them and clarifies the continuous distance gradient along the receding table plane. However, the map is unreliable on flat or reflective surfaces, rendering the closed laptop lid nearly flush with the table, blurring the facial features and head orientation of the nearby person into a flat silhouette, and losing detail in the dark background on the far left.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies the main foreground and mid-ground components: the dining table in front of and below the camera wearer (0.3 to 1.2 m), the primary seated person across the table (1.2 to 1.5 m, about 3 m from the far-left person), a distant person and couch on the far left in frames 1 and 2 (3 to 5 m), various bottles, cups, and laptops on the tabletop (0.4 to 1.1 m), a microwave on the shelf behind the main person in frame 3 (about 2.2 m), and a potted plant/basket by the right window (about 2.5 m). It shows the main person's upper torso directly behind the table edge—with their lower body occluded by the table and their right leg propped up on the left—while foreground bottles and cups sit within the camera wearer's reach (0.4 to 0.8 m) and two laptops lie within reach of the seated person and camera wearer (0.8 to 1.1 m), separated by the central water bottle. Across the five frames, as the camera wearer pans right, the far-left person and couch masks disappear after frame 2, the main person and dining table shift from center to left, and a partially visible appliance enters on the far right edge in frame 5 (about 0.8 m away). This map makes it easier than RGB to isolate discrete object boundaries—such as distinguishing the open dark laptop in front of the seated person in frame 1 and the distant person on the far-left armchair—amidst heavy visual clutter. However, it is frequently unreliable: it misses the dining table mask entirely in frame 4, mislabels the paper-towel roll as a chair in frame 4, misclassifies the window basket as a potted plant or bowl and the right-edge washing machine as a TV, leaves many tabletop jars unsegmented, and provides no internal detail to tell whether the person faces the camera wearer or looks away.
descriptions.pose: The pose map isolates the upper-body skeleton (yellow) and left hand (magenta) of the person seated across the table at roughly 1.2 to 1.5 m in front of the camera wearer, while the distant person on the far left (4 to 5 m away) is not detected at all. In frames 1 through 3, the shoulders, elbows, and wrists show the seated person leaning slightly forward over the table with both hands within reach of the cards and dark laptop directly in front of their torso (about 0.9 to 1.2 m from the camera wearer), while their lower body below the hips is largely occluded by the table except for a raised right knee on the left side. The head keypoints (eyes, ears, nose) indicate that the person faces downward and slightly toward the camera wearer in frame 1, then turns their head sharply to their right (the camera's left, looking away from the camera wearer toward the far-left room) in frames 2 and 3. This skeletal wireframe makes the exact 3D articulation of the shoulder-elbow-wrist chain, the fine finger cluster of the left hand resting on the table, and the head rotation between frames 1 and 3 much clearer than in the dark maroon hoodie of the RGB image. However, the pose map is highly unreliable in frames 4 and 5: in frame 4 it outputs a corrupted, horizontally sideways body skeleton with no hand keypoints even though the person is still seated upright on the left, and in frame 5 it fails completely, detecting zero keypoints even as the person turns their head back toward the table.
